keyVerseText: I shall see him, but not now: I shall behold him, but not nigh: there shall come a Star out of Jacob, and a Sceptre shall rise out of Israel, and shall smite the corners of Moab, and destroy all the children of Sheth . smite: or, smite through the princes of
rootMeaning: The Hebrew root קוּר (qûwr) is a primitive root that also derives from the related noun קִיר (qîyr), meaning wall or side. This connection suggests a foundational sense of constructing or shaping boundaries, whether by digging trenches or building walls. The root thus conveys actions involving breaking down or casting out as well as creating protective structures, highlighting a dynamic interplay between destruction and construction beyond the simple English glosses of 'dig' or 'destroy.'
usageInScripture: Across its six occurrences, קוּר consistently involves physical actions such as digging or casting out, with the most frequent translations being 'I have digged' and 'casteth out.' The verb also carries connotations of destruction or breaking down, showing a semantic range from literal excavation to figurative removal or devastation. This variety reveals the word’s flexibility in describing both constructive and destructive divine or human acts.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding קוּר enriches our grasp of God’s sovereign activity in Scripture, where He both creates and judges—digging wells to sustain life and casting out or destroying to enact justice. The root’s dual sense of building and breaking reflects the biblical tension between God’s mercy and holiness. Christ’s redemptive work can be seen as a fulfillment of this dynamic, bringing restoration where there was ruin and breaking down the barriers of sin to establish a new covenant community.
keyVerseReflection: In Numbers 24:17, the prophecy speaks of a Star and Sceptre arising from Israel that will 'smite the corners of Moab, and destroy all the children of Sheth.' The word קוּר here emphasizes the decisive and powerful action of breaking down the enemy’s strongholds. This imagery underscores the Messiah’s authority to overcome opposition, fulfilling God’s promise to establish His kingdom through Christ’s victorious reign.
